          <p>As will be outlined further, the dynamics of the golf swing are dependent on not only what you are currently doing, but also what you have done in the past—a phenomenon known as "drift" in nonlinear control theory. <section id="mission" class="mission-section">
  <div class="container">
    <div class="mission-content">
      <p class="mission-text">
        AffineDrift is named after a concept in nonlinear control theory, the mathematical framework for managing complex, chaotic systems. The structure of a control-affine system allows the total movement to be clearly separated into two distinct components:
      </p>
      <ul class="mission-list">
        <li><strong>Drift:</strong> The system's inherent, autonomous motion based on its current state.</li>
        <li><strong>Control:</strong> The changes in motion that arise only from deliberate, external inputs.</li>
      </ul>
      <p class="mission-text">
        This division reveals a profound truth: history matters. The system's past actions are encoded in its present state—its accumulated momentum, geometry, and timing. For the golfer, the implication is that every swing is a combination of your current, conscious effort and the powerful inertia of everything that has come before. As Marcus Aurelius noted, the past is always writing itself into the present.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="theory" class="theory-section">
  <div class="container">
    <div class="theory-content">
      <div class="theory-intro">
        <p>
          We model the golf swing as a <strong>nonlinear control-affine system</strong>. This formulation bridges
          multibody dynamics (Newton–Euler / Lagrangian mechanics) and geometric control theory.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="coordination-section">
        <h3>Coordination as Trajectory Optimization</h3>
        <p>
          The golf swing is a problem of <strong>underactuated nonlinear control</strong>. The golfer must coordinate
          a high-dimensional multibody system (torso, arms, club) to achieve a precise end-effector state (impact)
          subject to biomechanical constraints.
        </p>
        <p>
          From a Lagrangian perspective, the motion is governed by the principle of least action, modified by non-conservative
          forces (muscular torques). The golfer's nervous system effectively solves a <strong>trajectory optimization</strong> problem:
          finding a control policy \(u(t)\) that minimizes a cost function (e.g., effort, error) while satisfying the
          system dynamics \(\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u\).
        </p>
        <p>
          The complexity arises from the <strong>nonlinearity</strong> of the inertia matrix \(M(q)\) and the Coriolis/centrifugal
          terms \(C(q,\dot{q})\). However, the <strong>affine structure</strong> reveals that at any instantaneous state \(x\),
          the effect of muscular effort is linear. This allows us to rigorously separate the "drift" (what happens passively)
          from the "input" (what is actively forced).
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="math-block">
        <h3>Mathematical Derivation</h3>
        <p>
          Consider the golfer and club as a rigid-body system with generalized coordinates \(q \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
          The equations of motion are given by the standard manipulator equation:
        </p>
        <div class="equation">
          \[ M(q)\ddot{q} + C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + G(q) = B(q)u \]
        </div>
        <div class="equation-explanation">
            <p>where:</p>
            <ul>
                <li>\(M(q)\) is the positive-definite <strong>inertia matrix</strong>.</li>
                <li>\(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q}\) represents <strong>Coriolis and centrifugal forces</strong>.</li>
                <li>\(G(q)\) is the <strong>gravitational vector</strong>.</li>
                <li>\(u \in \mathbb{R}^m\) is the vector of active muscle torques.</li>
                <li>\(B(q)\) maps active torques to generalized forces.</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <p>
            To obtain the state-space form, we solve for acceleration \(\ddot{q}\):
        </p>
        <div class="equation">
            \[ \ddot{q} = M(q)^{-1} \Big[ B(q)u - C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} - G(q) \Big] \]
        </div>

        <p>
            Defining the state vector \(x = [q^T, \dot{q}^T]^T\), we derive the control-affine form:
        </p>
        <div class="equation">
          \[\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u\]
        </div>

        <div class="equation-explanation">
          <p>Here, the <strong>Drift Vector Field</strong> \(f(x)\) encapsulates all passive dynamics:</p>
          <div class="equation" style="font-size: 1rem; padding: 1rem;">
             \[ f(x) = \begin{bmatrix} \dot{q} \\ -M^{-1}(q)(C(q,\dot{q})\dot{q} + G(q)) \end{bmatrix} \]
          </div>
          <p>And the <strong>Control Vector Field</strong> \(g(x)\) defines the system's receptivity to input:</p>
          <div class="equation" style="font-size: 1rem; padding: 1rem;">
             \[ g(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ M^{-1}(q)B(q) \end{bmatrix} \]
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>

      <div class="key-properties">
        <div class="g-term-explanation">
          <h3>Mechanical Interpretation</h3>
          <p>
            The term \(g(x)\) involves the inverse inertia matrix \(M^{-1}(q)\). This implies that the
            <strong>mechanical advantage</strong> of a muscle depends heavily on the body's configuration.
            A torque applied at the shoulder has a different effect on the clubhead depending on the wrist angle
            due to the changing moment of inertia. The affine framework makes this configuration-dependent
            coupling explicit.
          </p>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<section id="golf" class="golf-section">
  <div class="container">
    <div class="golf-content">
      <div class="golf-intro">
        <p>
          By framing the swing as a control-affine system, we move beyond static positions to analyze the flow of
          dynamics. We can explicitly calculate the contribution of passive physics versus active intent.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="golf-model">
        <h3>System Components</h3>
        <div class="components-grid">
          <div class="component">
            <h4>State Space \(x\)</h4>
            <p> \(\mathbb{R}^{2n}\) vector containing all joint angles and velocities.</p>
          </div>
          <div class="component">
            <h4>Drift \(f(x)\)</h4>
            <p>The "natural" path of the swing if muscles went silent. Dominated by centrifugal loads and gravity.</p>
          </div>
          <div class="component">
            <h4>Control \(u\)</h4>
            <p>The active muscular intervention. Limited by force-velocity properties and neural reaction times.</p>
          </div>
           <div class="component">
            <h4>Input Field \(g(x)\)</h4>
            <p>The configuration-dependent map from torques to accelerations, weighted by the inverse inertia matrix.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>

    </div>
  </div>
</section>
